result:
There's a drawer in everyone's mind that doesn't close all the way.

You know the one. You push it shut and it slides back open an inch, just enough to show you the corner of something inside. An old movie ticket. A name you haven't said out loud in five years. The exact way the light fell on a Tuesday afternoon when you were nine and you had no idea you were supposed to be remembering it forever.

I've been thinking about that drawer a lot.

We talk about big moments like they are the architecture of our lives - graduations, moves, first kisses, last goodbyes, the job offer, the diagnosis. We build our autobiographies out of them because they are easy to point to. *This happened, then this happened.* But I'm not sure we actually *live* in the big moments. I think we live in the hallways between them.

We live in the 4:37 p.m. on a random Wednesday when you're waiting for the microwave to finish and you're staring out the window and for a half-second you feel completely, inexplicably okay. We live in the way your friend laughs when they're trying not to laugh. We live in the specific weight of grocery bags on your fingers, in the sound of a distant lawnmower through a screen door in July, in the way cold air smells different at 6 a.m. than it does at midnight.

It's strange, isn't it? How the brain is so bad at remembering what we tell it to remember, and so good at remembering what we never asked it to keep.

I remember once, I was on a train that was delayed. It was winter. The kind of winter where the sky is not really a sky but a flat, white lid. Everyone was annoyed. People sighing, checking phones, coats still on because the heating wasn't quite working. Across from me, a woman was trying to keep a toddler occupied. He was maybe two, in this enormous puffy snowsuit that made his arms stick out like a starfish. He had a little board book that he kept dropping, and every time he dropped it she would pick it up, and he would drop it again, and she would pick it up again, with a patience that seemed impossible.

At one point he just stared out the window at the snow coming down sideways, and he said, clear as anything, "More sky is falling."

More sky is falling.

And the woman laughed, this tired, beautiful laugh, and said, "Yeah, baby, a little more sky is falling."

Nobody else on that train heard it. Or if they did, they forgot it by the next stop. But I've carried it for years. I carry it because it was true. That's exactly what snow is. It's more sky falling. And only a kid who hasn't learned the separate word for it yet would be honest enough to say it.

We forget that we are always translating the world into smaller, dumber words.

I think about translation a lot. How you can never really tell someone what it felt like to be you in a moment. You can describe it, you can approximate it, you can say "I was sad" or "I was happy" but those words are buckets and the feeling is an ocean. "Sad" can mean you cried in a parking lot because a song came on, or that you didn't get out of bed for three days, or that you watched someone you love pack their things into boxes. Same word. Different planets.

So we do this thing where we gesture wildly at each other with language, hoping something lands. We say "Do you know what I mean?" constantly, and we mean *Please tell me I'm not alone in here.*

You aren't. You're not.

Here is a secret that took me a long time to learn: almost everyone is worried they are doing being a person wrong.

They think there is a correct way to be 27, or 42, or 19. A correct way to grieve, to love, to succeed. They think other people got the manual and they missed the orientation day. They look at other people's lives on their phones and think those lives are smooth and continuous, while their own feels like a series of drafts and outtakes.

But the truth is, nobody's life is smooth. Everybody's film has jump cuts. Everybody has at least one story they tell differently depending on who is asking. Everybody has apologized to someone in their head a thousand times who never heard it. Everybody has forgiven someone who never apologized.

And everybody - even the most cynical, eye-rolling person you know - has at least one thing that can still make them feel wonder without trying. The way the moon looks too big some nights. The way dogs dream and their paws twitch. The way a song you haven't heard in a decade can put you instantly back in a specific car, on a specific road, with the windows down.

Wonder is not childish. Wonder is a survival skill.

I used to think adulthood meant you stopped believing in magic. Now I think it means you have to *find* magic on purpose, because the world will not hand it to you anymore. You have to notice it. You have to protect it a little. You have to be the one who says "look, more sky is falling" when everyone else just says "it's snowing."

Maybe that's all faith is. Deciding to be the translator instead of the cynic.

If I had to leave you with one image - since I have all these words and I want to use them well - it would be this:

Picture a house at night, but not a scary house, a lived-in house. Kitchen light on. It's raining. Inside, someone is doing the dishes. Not because they love doing dishes, but because the dishes need doing. And outside the window, the rain is hitting the glass, and the person doing the dishes pauses for just a second to watch a single raindrop take a winding, completely unique path down the pane. It zig-zags. It merges with another drop. It hesitates. It finally disappears.

And for that one second, the person isn't thinking about bills or tomorrow or what they said three years ago that they wish they could take back. They are just watching the drop. They are just here.

That is enough. That has always been enough.

We spend so much of our lives waiting to feel like we've finally arrived - at happiness, at certainty, at being the person we want to be. But arrival is not a place you pull into. It's these seconds. It's the drawer that won't close. It's the more sky falling. It's the raindrop and the kitchen light.

You are not behind. You are not lost. You are in the hallway, and the hallway *is* the house.

So if today is ordinary, let it be ordinary. Let it be small and quiet and not particularly photogenic. Water your plants. Text someone you miss. Look up at the sky for five seconds longer than you need to.

Notice one thing you were going to miss.

That is how you write a life. Not in big, perfect sentences, but in quiet, true ones.

And if no one has told you lately - the fact that you are still here, still trying to translate your ocean into buckets for someone else to understand - that is brave. That is quietly, completely brave.

Keep going.
